html_en:
Agentic AI is moving from demo to daily workflow faster than almost anyone predicted — and the debate is shifting from whether agents work to how to measure their value and what happens to jobs when they do.

The Metric That Died: Why $/Token Is Out and $/Task Is In

One of the sharpest observations of the week came from Shawn Wang (@swyx), who declared a quiet death in how we think about AI economics:

"$ per input/output tokens died as a relevant cost measure sometime last year. If you haven't updated your x axes to $/task per @ArtificialAnlys, then idk if you can be taken seriously anymore these days." — @swyx

It's a pointed but fair critique. As models become capable of completing multi-step, multi-hour tasks autonomously, pricing them by the token is like pricing a contractor by how many keystrokes they type. Guillermo Rauch (@rauchg) implicitly backed this up with benchmark data from Vercel, noting that on cybersecurity tasks, Grok 4.5 has emerged as a compelling price-performance leader:

"Grok 4.5 has emerged as the best cybersecurity AI model on price-performance. It's 10x cheaper than Sol, 5.7x cheaper than Opus 5, and 2.2x cheaper than Kimi K3, yet at Kimi-like perf. Sol remains the frontier, ahead of Opus 5." — @rauchg

What's being measured now is outcomes per dollar — and that's a fundamentally different market.

Codex in the Wild: The Bike Ride That Shipped a Video

OpenAI's Codex agent is generating genuine field reports from power users, and they're compelling. Peter Yang (@petergyang) surfaced a story from Jason Liu (@jxnlco), DevEx at OpenAI, that captures what autonomous agents actually feel like when they work:

"I was on a bike ride when a coworker asked me to fix a launch video. So I connected remotely from my phone and asked Codex to use computer use to edit the video, export it, and post it back to Slack. Twenty minutes later, there was a new video in the Slack thread. Then I told Codex: 'Every 30 minutes, check the thread for feedback and export V2, V3, V4.' By the time I got home, the launch video was greenlit." — Jason Liu, via @petergyang

Watch/Listen: Full interview with Jason Liu on Codex workflows

Meanwhile, @thsottiaux at OpenAI was celebrating the fast adoption of ChatGPT Work with an impromptu usage limit reset for paid users — a small but telling signal that enterprise uptake is outpacing expectations. And on the infrastructure side, @steipete flagged a glimpse of agent-to-agent collaboration in the wild:

"My agent reported a bug, their agent fixed it. [in the same night] @jarredsumner's robobun setup is future." — @steipete

Kimi K3, Sandbox Security, and the Infrastructure Layer Nobody Talks About

With Kimi K3 weights now public — confirmed by Aaron Levie (@levie) with a simple "The k3 weights have arrived" — the open-source frontier continues to compress the gap with proprietary labs. But Rauch raised a less-discussed implication of running powerful agents: the security boundary matters more than almost anyone has planned for.

"Kimi's paper underlines the importance of the right security boundary for agents to run in. tl;dr: container-level isolation is not enough. In their experiments, agents crashed the underlying machine (via kernel panics). Firecracker microVMs (as in Vercel Sandbox) are safe." — @rauchg

This is the kind of unglamorous-but-critical infrastructure detail that separates production-grade agent deployment from a clever demo. As agents get more powerful, the blast radius of a runaway process grows — and kernel panics are a memorable way to learn that lesson.

What Comes After the First Wave of AI Apps

The AI & I podcast from Every this week featured a conversation between Dan Shipper and Chris, cofounder and CEO of Granola — the AI meeting notes app that helped define what "AI-native productivity" could look like. The episode is a thoughtful meditation on what it means to build in a category that gets immediately commoditized. Watch/Listen: The Founder of a $1.5B AI Company on What Comes After the First Wave of AI Apps

"Meeting notes are not the end all, be all value that everyone's running after. There's something much bigger. I think we are in the very, very early steps of a computing revolution. What has come thus far will pale in comparison to what will come soon." — Chris, Granola CEO

His framing on competition is refreshingly honest — not the usual founder-speak about "not thinking about competitors." When Notion, OpenAI, and Zoom all copy your core feature, you either find the next thing or you don't:

"Just because people use us today doesn't mean they're going to use us for that in the future if we're not the best at that next thing... What people are fighting for today doesn't matter. There's this incredible opportunity ahead."

It's the right mental model for any AI product company right now. Features get cloned in weeks. Distribution and the ability to keep finding the next frontier is the actual moat.

Jevons Is Showing Up in Hiring Data

The jobs-and-AI debate got a grounded data point from Aaron Levie, who's talking to enterprises across industries:

"The negative AI jobs outcome just continues to not be happening as some predicted. A large portion of enterprises I talk with — across industries — are still hiring, just with a tilt in the kind of roles they're going after... They're hiring engineers to go after problems they couldn't tackle before. They're hiring in sales because they can go deeper in client relationships now with the help of AI... Anyone using AI merely to cut costs eventually just gets outcompeted by companies that use AI to better serve their customers." — @levie

The Jevons paradox — where efficiency gains increase total consumption rather than reduce it — is a useful lens here. Cheaper, faster software development doesn't mean fewer developers; it means more software gets built. We're early enough in this cycle that the expansion effect is still dominating the substitution effect. Whether that holds as agents become truly autonomous remains the most important open question in the industry.
html_zh:
当AI编码助手开始在骑行途中完成视频剪辑任务，当Kimi K3权重悄然开放、成本战进入新维度——今天的行业信号指向同一个方向：AI代理时代已不是未来，而是此刻正在发生的日常。

🚴 Codex的骑行时刻：代理工作流的新基准

本周最令人印象深刻的AI使用案例，来自一次普通的自行车骑行。Peter Yang 在采访中记录了OpenAI开发者体验负责人 Jason Liu 的亲身经历：

"我在骑车时，同事让我修改一个发布视频。于是我用手机远程连接，让Codex用computer use功能剪辑视频、导出并发回Slack。二十分钟后，新视频出现在了Slack线程里。然后我告诉Codex：'每隔30分钟检查一次线程反馈，导出V2、V3、V4。'等我到家时，发布视频已经获批。"
— @petergyang 引述 @jxnlco

这不是科幻故事，这是一个工程师在骑行途中完成的真实工作流。Watch/Listen: 完整采访视频。与此同时，OpenAI产品负责人 @thsottiaux 宣布为庆祝ChatGPT Work的快速普及，重置了所有付费用户的使用限额，引发广泛欢呼。

📊 成本战升维：$/任务取代$/token

Kimi K3权重发布，迅速在性价比榜上掀起波澜。Vercel CEO Guillermo Rauch 援引最新基准数据指出：

"在我们最新的网络安全AI模型性价比评测中，Grok 4.5异军突起：比Sol便宜10倍，比Opus 5便宜5.7倍，比Kimi K3便宜2.2倍，但性能与Kimi持平。Sol仍然是前沿，领先于Opus 5。"
— @rauchg

而 swyx 则一针见血地点出了更深层的范式转移：

"每输入/输出token的价格作为相关成本衡量标准，已经在去年某个时候死去了。如果你还没有把评测的X轴更新为'每任务成本（$/task）'，老实说，现在很难被认真对待。"
— @swyx

这是一个简单但重要的信号：竞争的维度已经从"模型多便宜"转向"完成一件事要花多少钱"。

🏢 代理基础设施的安全边界

随着AI代理承担越来越多真实任务，"把它跑在哪里"变成了一个严肃的工程问题。Rauch 引用Kimi的研究论文警告：

"Kimi的论文强调了代理运行时正确安全边界的重要性。简而言之：容器级隔离是不够的。在他们的实验中，代理导致了底层机器崩溃（内核panic）。Firecracker microVM（如Vercel Sandbox中使用的）才是安全的。"
— @rauchg

另一边，@steipete 分享了一个更令人兴奋的场景："我的代理报告了一个bug，他们的代理当晚就修复了。" ——代理对代理的协作，正在从概念变成日常。

💼 AI与就业：Jevons悖论正在上演

Box CEO Aaron Levie 对当前企业AI采用的观察，提供了一个冷静而乐观的视角，反驳了"AI消灭工作岗位"的悲观叙事：

"我交流过的大量企业——横跨各行各业——仍在招聘，只是招聘的岗位类型有所倾斜。他们发现AI让他们能做更多的事，Jevons悖论正在真实发生。他们雇佣工程师去攻克之前无法触及的问题，在销售端招人因为AI帮他们深化客户关系，在内部招聘FDE来部署AI。仅仅用AI削减成本的公司，最终会被那些用AI更好服务客户、推动业务突破的公司所超越。"
— @levie

🎙️ 对话：AI第一波应用之后，然后呢？

Watch/Listen: Every AI & I播客：估值15亿美元的AI公司创始人谈第一波AI应用之后的世界

Granola联合创始人兼CEO Chris在与 Dan Shipper 的对话中，提供了一个发人深省的长线视角。面对"会议记录"这一赛道被Notion、OpenAI、Zoom纷纷复制的现实，他的回应出人意料地淡然：

"我认为我们正处于一场计算革命极其早期的阶段，迄今为止发生的一切，与即将到来的相比将黯然失色。会议记录并不是所有人真正争夺的终极价值。有更大的东西——那就是在AI原生世界里，我们用什么界面工作、如何工作。当我想到竞争时，我觉得人们今天争夺的东西并不重要，前方有巨大的机会。"

创业依然是刀光剑影的厮杀——不管顺境还是逆境。但那些把眼光放得足够长远的人，或许正是下一波浪潮的弄潮儿。
